1126933235688414443.desc: We show you one of the best heritage of cultural tourism, as known The Khan's Palace. In the Crimean heartland, the longest-lived of the Turkic khanates left an even more enduring landmark, The Khan's Palace; in other words, home to the Crimean Tatars. Raised in the 16th century, Khan’s Palace served as a palace for the representatives of the Giray dynasty. Located in the city of Bakhchisaray, the palace was the political, spiritual, and cultural epicenter of the Crimean Tatars. Above all, n the the Palace has the limestone mountains, pristine forest slopes, and orchards.Khan's Palace is a complex containing majestic mosques, menacing courtrooms, a hidden harem, a fountain of tears, and sorrowful tombs. The earliest dated construction in this ensemble bears the date of 1532, while the written records mention the Palace under 1539.The Palace stretches more than 50000 square meters and consists of 17 buildings and 9 courtyards. So,the overall architectural ambiance of the Palace is a careful amalgam of Middle Eastern and Crimean Tatar tradition. Moreover gardens and a life-giving, sustaining, and purifying supply of water is the focal point of the Palace’s design. The Big Khan Mosque is one of the oldest structures in the Palace, dating back to 1532, in short of the best heritage of cultural tourism. The Mosque is one of the largest in Crimea and bears the name of Sahib I Giray as its commissioner. The entry into the mosque is from a portal facing north. In addition, the mosque is made by Ottoman-designed. The roof, a narthex, and porticos are covering the main prayer hall. From the porticos, rise two minarets to the height of 28 meters.The minarets are octagonal and adorned with conical tops and finials. The lead and glass are decorating the minarets with imitation stones. The walls of the Mosque contain murals; depicting Quranic inscriptions and Islamic symbology. The calligraphic adeptness of these murals is phenomenal and bears a proud testimony to the skills of Persian artists. To sum up, the murals appear in green cartouches on the main façade of the Mosque and add to the charm of wood and plasterwork.

1127113118506818371.desc: In this episode, we head to Baima Snow Mountain Nature Reserve in Diqing Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province, to learn about and participate in the conservation work for the rare and precious national treasure: the Yunnan snub-nosed monkey. The presenter ventures into the forest, experiences the daily life of local forest rangers, and witnesses the harmonious relationship between humans and monkeys. We interview "the Monkey Father" - Long Yongcheng, chief scientist of The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and leader of China's Primate Expert Group - who shares stories about the two decades of efforts dedicated to protecting the Yunnan snub-nosed monkey. We also go to the mountains to conduct research alongside young volunteers. Through these activities, we recognize the importance of environmental education for young people in promoting natural ecological balance and harmonious development.

1127113118506818372.desc: The final episode traces the cross-ocean transmission of Shandong Mantis Style. In the mountains of northern Italy, host Kleber visits Dante Basili, a veteran Italian practitioner in his sixties, who recounts travelling to China 36 years ago to learn Mantis Style and returning home to teach Chinese martial arts ever since. Kleber then heads to Shandong to meet Yu Bo and Yu Tao, sons of Mantis Style grandmaster Yu Hai. He witnesses a traditional apprenticeship ceremony and explores the style's fighting essence: adopting its spirit rather than merely copying its form. The episode shows how Mantis Style has taken root and flourished in different cultural settings. Ultimately, this journey across Europe and Asia suggests that transmission is not only about techniques, but also about dialogue across time and distance, and a shared resonance of spirit between cultures.

From packed stadium shows to sold-out performances in smaller cities, China's live music scene is expanding rapidly. Young audiences are turning concerts into a cultural routine: traveling across cities, sharing the experience online and building collective memories around live performances.

The boom now extends far beyond the stage, boosting tourism, retail spending and local economies. In this episode of Unboxing China, we explore how concerts are reshaping consumption patterns and becoming a new driver of cultural and urban development.

1127294327484651434.desc:
For months, Chinese social feeds have been filled with "Lao Ji"- a third-person way of saying "me." What began as a slang sign-off, "Love you, Lao Ji. See you tomorrow," now signals a broader shift toward self-care and emotional self-support. It also feeds a  huge market where young consumers are rechanneling budgets toward small, meaningful purchases that support emotional wellbeing.

In this episode of Unboxing China, we trace how a casual phrase turned into a cultural movement, reshaping consumption and mental-health talk.

The Token Economy
Demand for AI tokens is surging, with trends like “tokenmaxxing” accelerating the race for computing power.
As pressure mounts on computing and energy infrastructure, China is leveraging its clean energy strengths to support AI growth, while “token exports” emerge as a new way to deliver AI services to global users.
What’s the future like for the “token economy”? Join us on BizTalk as we explore the economics behind the AI revolution.

1127294327484651437.desc:
For a thousand years, Jingdezhen's kiln fires have shaped iconic ceramics and a living cultural heritage.

In this episode of Living with AI, CGTN reporter He Jingyi explores how AI can help preserve ancient craftsmanship -- and how governance can keep pace when the oldest traditions meet the newest technology.
